name: North Tanna
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Primary stress is invariably on the penultimate syllable in Erromango. In Anejom and the Tanna languages, it is normally penultimate, but (a) final if the vowel of the final syllable is long, and (b) antepenultimate in certain very restricted contexts. Secondary stress normally occurs two syllables to the left of the primary-stressed syllable. [p. 9] ... it does not match the facts of the daughter languages, all of which have regular penultimate stress, irrespective of whether the final syllable was open or closed. [p. 117]
new_statements.citation: Lynch, John. 2001. The linguistic history of southern Vanuatu. Pacific Linguistics 509. Canberra: Australian National University.
new_statements.locator: §1.5.2 'Vowels, phonotactics and stress', p. 9 (PDF p. 21); supporting passage §4.4.3, p. 117 (PDF p. 129)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; a long vowel in the final syllable attracts stress to the final syllable; a few very restricted contexts (not specified for North Tanna) give antepenultimate stress. Statement is made for 'the Tanna languages' as a group (North Tanna, Whitesands, Lenakel, Southwest Tanna, Kwamera), with North Tanna data from Lynch's own field notes.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress normally two syllables to the left of the primary-stressed syllable (alternating leftward).
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress when the final-syllable vowel is long (vowel length is contrastive, mostly in final syllables); antepenultimate stress 'in certain very restricted contexts' (not enumerated); p. 137 notes Lenakel (not North Tanna) shows 'compensatory lengthening/irregular final stress' in a loan. No North Tanna-specific exceptions given.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in a comparative-historical monograph's synchronic overview of the Southern Vanuatu languages; covers the five Tanna languages collectively rather than North Tanna alone; no North Tanna examples with stress marked are given.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is for 'the Tanna languages' collectively (North Tanna nort2847, Whitesands whit1245, Lenakel lena1238, Southwest Tanna sout2869, Kwamera kwam1252), not a North Tanna-only section; Lynch's North Tanna data come from his own notes on one dialect (the one with prenasalised stops), while 'some dialects of North Tanna (see e.g. Blaymires 1995)' have the Lenakel-type inventory (Lynch 2001: 7). Lynch & Crowley 2001: 125 note the boundaries between North Tanna, Lenakel and Whitesands are 'fuzzy' and may form a continuum. Sverredal 2018 is based on the North Tanna New Testament (Carlson translation) and is silent on stress.

sources.note: §1.5.2 'Vowels, phonotactics and stress', p. 9: in Anejom and the (five) Tanna languages primary stress is normally penultimate, but final if the final-syllable vowel is long, antepenultimate in certain very restricted contexts; secondary stress two syllables to the left of primary. North Tanna is one of the five Tanna languages (Table 1.2, p. 4: data source 'own notes'). §4.4.3 p. 117 repeats that all modern SV daughter languages have regular penultimate stress irrespective of final-syllable closure. Group-level statement, not a North Tanna-specific section.
